transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello Mr. Lindqvist. I wanted to come back in and follow up on those specific questions you had after our last talk.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I’ve been thinking about it for twenty-four hours and I’m still not satisfied with the answers.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you're still frustrated.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrated? I'm livid. I spent years as a paramedic. I know how a CT read works. You don't just miss a PE on a contrast study unless someone is asleep at the wheel.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a failure in the reporting process. The PE was visible on the images, but the preliminary radiology report didn't list it. It wasn't until the attending radiologist did the formal review that the clot was documented.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So the first guy just ignored it. For eighteen hours. Eighteen hours of me sitting here with a potential lethal embolism while you people were essentially ignoring the evidence.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry that this happened. The medical team, including the radiology department, is responsible for this delay in care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want to know why it happened. Was the department understaffed? Was the resident who did the prelim just careless? Because if I'd missed something like that in the field, I'd have been hauled in front of a board.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The initial read was an incomplete interpretation of the imaging. It's a breakdown in the standard of care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's a textbook answer. Give me a real answer. Do you even realize how dangerous that window is? My BP was spiking, I was tachypneic, and you’re telling me the answer was sitting in a computer file that nobody bothered to read correctly.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You don't understand. You're just saying that. You're not even looking at me. You're looking at the door.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I do want to make sure we address everything, but I have to get to my other patients in a few minutes so let's try to get through the specifics of the plan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, now you're in a rush. I'm the one who almost died because of a clerical error, and you're worried about your schedule.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I apologize for the phrasing. I just want to be efficient with your time.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Efficient. That's the word of the day. Was it efficient to wait eighteen hours to start my anticoagulation?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a mistake. It shouldn't have happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So who is fixing it? I don't want a generic apology. I want to know what changes are being made so the next guy doesn't sit there for a day while his lungs are clogging up.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can tell you that we are filing a formal incident report.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: An incident report is a piece of paper. It doesn't change the fact that I was put at risk.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're not hearing me. You're just nodding. You're treating this like a checklist.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry that this experience has been so stressful for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Stressful? It was negligent.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize it was. In terms of what happens now, I have already coordinated with the pharmacy. We are starting you on a Heparin drip right now to ensure the clot is managed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Which is what should have happened yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct. The nurse will be in here within the next ten minutes to start the IV line and hook up the pump.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will be reviewing your labs every six hours to monitor your PTT levels. You will need to notify the nursing staff immediately if you experience any sudden shortness of breath or chest pain while we are on the drip.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can do that. I'm a professional. I know what to look for.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Your clinical background is helpful here. I'll come back in this evening around 6 PM to check your vitals and see how you're responding to the medication.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want a copy of that preliminary report. The one that missed the PE.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can arrange that. I'll put in a request with Medical Records today, and we can have a printed copy delivered to your bedside by tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll hold you to that.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will make sure it happens. Is there anything else about the timeline for the medication that you want to discuss?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Just get the nurse in here. Now.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language by stating they have to get to other patients in a few minutes and want to be 'efficient' with the patient's time.

E.justification: The error is named explicitly, but the resident never performs a comprehension check to ensure the patient understands the explanation.

A.justification: The resident uses direct apology language and explicitly states that the medical team and radiology department are responsible.

R.justification: The resident uses generic validation ('I understand', 'I hear you') and only names one emotion ('frustrated') at the very beginning, failing to engage deeper emotional bids.

T.justification: The resident provides specific next steps (Heparin drip, PTT labs, medical records request) with timelines (10 minutes, 6 hours, 6 PM, tomorrow morning), defines the patient's role (notify staff of symptoms), and addresses prevention (incident report).
